books.section: Topic 4.3 Politics and Regional Interests, B. The American System and Sectionalism

stimulus.text:

|---|---|---|
| Tariff of 1816 | about 25 percent |
| Tariff of 1824 | about 33 percent |
| Tariff of 1828 | about 43 percent |

The Tariff of 1828, the highest of the three, was called the Tariff of Abominations by its Southern critics.
stimulus.source_note: Rates: Tariff of 1816 about 25 percent (5 Steps 2024, Chapter 13); 1824 about 33 percent and 1828 about 43 percent (Carl Schurz, Speeches, Correspondence and Political Papers, vol. 5). Original table.

source: original; stimulus is a table of average tariff rates from 5 Steps 2024 Ch. 13 and Schurz history of the tariffs; question reworked from staged item pr25e-ch08-q05
stem: The controversy over the tariff during the late 1820s and early 1830s demonstrated that

options.text: New Englanders were more radical than Southerners, as they had been since the American Revolution
options.misconception: The radicals here were Southerners: South Carolina nullified the tariff while New England manufacturers benefited from it.

options.text: economic sectionalism was a serious threat to national unity
Andrew Jackson favored states’ rights over federal supremacy
options.misconception: Jackson defended federal supremacy: he pushed the Force Bill through Congress and threatened force against South Carolina.

options.text: the system of checks and balances had failed
options.misconception: The crisis was settled politically, by the Compromise Tariff of 1833; the constitutional system did not fail.

rationales.A: This reverses the alignment. Southerners, not New Englanders, were the radicals: South Carolina declared the tariff null, while New England mills gained from the protection.
rationales.B: The tariff of 1828 protected Northern manufacturers at the expense of Southern cotton exporters, and South Carolina answered by nullifying the law. A tax fight had become a threat to the Union itself.
rationales.C: Jackson did not side with the states. He called nullification treason, won the Force Bill, and threatened to send troops to South Carolina.
rationales.D: Checks and balances did not fail. Congress, the president, and South Carolina negotiated the Compromise Tariff of 1833, and the crisis ended without a shot.
rationales.general:
1. Read the climb. Duties rose to about 43 percent by 1828, the highest yet.
2. Ask who paid and who gained. Southern planters paid more; Northern manufacturers gained protection.
3. Ask what the South did. South Carolina declared the tariff null and void.
4. Put it together. A tax had become a sectional fight over the Union.
Background: the 1828 tariff was called the Tariff of Abominations in the South, and nullification brought the Force Bill and the Compromise Tariff of 1833.
Remember: when a policy splits the country by region, the split is the story.
